teaser: A painter signed the back wall of this bedroom like a witness. Nobody is sure what he witnessed.
review_notes:
Panel size 82.2 x 60 cm, three vertical oak boards.
Sitter: probably Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini (National Gallery's current view); the 1447 marriage document concerns his cousin Giovanni di Arrigo. Costanza Trenta, wife of Giovanni di Nicolao, was dead by February 1433.
Dog and chandelier painted without underdrawing (infrared study, National Gallery); the dog is absent from the mirror reflection.
Memorial theory (Margaret Koster, 2003): lit candle on his side, burnt-out candle stub on hers. The stub is not legible in the working image, so the lesson only points at the lit candle.
National Gallery purchase in 1842 for 600 pounds from Colonel James Hay; said to be the first Netherlandish painting bought by the Gallery.
Hat described as plaited straw dyed black; his tabard as silk velvet trimmed with fur; her gown wool lined with fur: per National Gallery technical descriptions.
Velazquez knowing the picture in the Madrid royal palace before painting Las Meninas (1656): widely accepted, not documented by him.
Cherry tree with fruit outside the window: present in the painting, very small in the working image (left edge, around x 0.08, y 0.27).

lesson.text: Three oak boards, glued edge to edge. Together they make a panel 82 centimeters high and 60 wide (about 32 by 24 inches), roughly the size of a pillowcase. On that small surface Jan van Eyck fitted a bedroom, two people, a dog, a brass chandelier and, in a mirror, the whole room a second time.

The year is 1434 and the city is Bruges, in today's Belgium, then one of the great markets of Europe. The man is probably Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini, an Italian merchant from Lucca who made his living there selling silk and other luxury cloth. The woman is his wife. Her name is where the trouble starts, and we will come back to it.

Van Eyck was court painter to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, the ruler of this region. When he signed a picture, he usually did it on the frame. Here he chose a stranger place, in the middle of the scene itself.
Jan van Eyck wrote his name inside this room. Where?

spots.title: Writing on the wall
spots.text: Above the mirror, in the flourished script of legal documents, a Latin line reads “Johannes de eyck fuit hic”, with the date 1434 beneath. It means: Jan van Eyck was here.

lesson.text: Not “Jan van Eyck made this”, the usual formula. “Was here.” It sounds like graffiti, or like a witness signing a contract. And if he was here, he should be somewhere in the room. The round mirror just under his name answers that.

lesson.title: Under the signature
lesson.text: The mirror is a convex one, bulging outward, so it gathers the entire room into a circle a few centimeters across.

spots.title: Two visitors
spots.text: You see the couple from behind, the window, the bed. Between them, in the doorway where you are standing, two tiny figures: one in blue, one in red. One of them is very likely the painter.

spots.title: Ten scenes
spots.text: The frame carries ten little roundels, each smaller than a fingernail on the real panel. They show the suffering and death of Christ, a full prayer cycle around a piece of household glass.

spots.title: Prayer beads
spots.text: A string of amber-colored beads hangs from a nail, each one catching the window light. Beads like these were counted while praying, and were a typical gift from a husband to a wife.

lesson.text: The mirror tells one small lie. The dog at the couple's feet does not appear in the reflection. Infrared imaging, which lets researchers see the drawing under the paint, shows the dog was never sketched in. Van Eyck added it late, straight in paint.

How do you paint a reflection that small? With oil. Van Eyck did not invent oil paint, as people long believed, but he pushed it further than anyone before him. He laid thin, see-through layers called glazes one over another, so light sinks into the color and comes back out, the way it does in glass or brass.
Van Eyck's revolution is patience. Layer after layer of transparent oil paint let him describe how light behaves on each material: fur, metal, wood, skin, glass.

That skill had a commercial use, and a cloth merchant knew it. Almost nothing in this room is there by chance. Read it the way a neighbor in Bruges would have: as a list of what these two could afford.

lesson.title: The price list
lesson.text: Four things a visitor in 1434 would have noticed at once.

spots.title: Oranges
spots.text: One on the windowsill, more on the chest below. Oranges did not grow in Flanders. They came by ship from the south and cost a small fortune, so leaving them lying around says a lot.

spots.title: Yards of green
spots.text: Her wool gown is lined with pale fur and so long that it pools on the floor. The sleeves are cut into rows of tiny leaf shapes. Every extra fold is cloth someone paid for.

spots.title: Hat and fur
spots.text: He wears a huge hat of plaited straw dyed black and a dark velvet cloak edged with brown fur from collar to hem. His face, pale and heavy-lidded, gives nothing away.

spots.title: Wooden clogs
spots.text: These are pattens, overshoes worn in the street to keep good shoes out of the mud. Kicked off in the corner, they are the most casual thing in a very controlled picture.

lesson.text: Outside the window, a cherry tree is in fruit, so it is summer. Yet both of them are wrapped in fur-lined layers. Comfort is not the issue. You dressed for a portrait in the most expensive things you owned.

The gown also explains the question every visitor asks. No, she is almost certainly not pregnant. She is gathering a heavy mass of fabric against her stomach, and a rounded belly was the fashionable silhouette of the day. Women saints who were never mothers are painted the same way.

Now the trouble. In 1934 the historian Erwin Panofsky argued that the panel is a painted marriage certificate: raised hand for the oath, joined hands, the painter signing as witness. It became the famous reading. Then archives showed that the Arnolfini long thought to be the sitter married in 1447, thirteen years too late.

So attention moved to his cousin, Giovanni di Nicolao. His wife, Costanza Trenta, had died by early 1433, a year before the date on the wall. Either he had remarried and no record survives, or this is a portrait of a living man and a dead wife. One object in the room is at the heart of that argument.
It is broad daylight, and yet something in the room is burning. Can you spot it?

spots.title: One candle
spots.text: The brass chandelier has room for several candles. A single one is lit, on the man's side. Some scholars read it as life on his side and none on hers. Others see the presence of God, or a custom for sealing an oath.

lesson.text: A flame that small now has to carry three rival theories, and that is typical of this painting. Van Eyck describes each thing so exactly that it feels like evidence, and then he does not tell you what case is being made.

The panel traveled. By 1516 it belonged to Margaret of Austria, later it hung in the royal palace in Madrid, and after the Napoleonic wars in Spain it turned up in the hands of a Scottish officer. The National Gallery bought it in 1842 for 600 pounds.

In Madrid, a court painter named Diego Velázquez could study it. In 1656 he painted “Las Meninas”, where a mirror on the back wall reflects people standing in the viewer's place. In London two centuries later, the young Pre-Raphaelite painters fell for its sharp detail and filled their own pictures with convex mirrors.
A wedding, a business arrangement, a memorial to a wife who died, or a rich couple showing off their front room? The wall only says that Jan was here. It does not say why he came.

quiz.question: What does the Latin line on the back wall say?
quiz.explanation: “Johannes de eyck fuit hic” means Jan van Eyck was here, followed by the date 1434.

quiz.question: What appears in the convex mirror that you cannot see in the room?
options: Two small figures in the doorway
quiz.explanation: The mirror shows two visitors, one in blue and one in red, standing where the viewer stands.

quiz.question: Why does the woman look pregnant?
options: The panel was damaged and repainted
She holds up heavy fabric, and a rounded belly was fashionable
quiz.explanation: She gathers her long gown against her stomach in the fashionable silhouette of the time.

quiz.question: What are glazes?
options: Thin, transparent layers of oil paint
Sheets of glass placed over a painting
quiz.explanation: Van Eyck built up color with thin see-through layers of oil paint called glazes.

quiz.question: Why did the oranges signal wealth?
options: They were imported from the south and very costly
Only nobles were allowed to eat them
quiz.explanation: Oranges did not grow in Flanders and arrived by ship at great expense.

quiz.question: Which later painter used a mirror on a back wall after knowing this picture in Madrid?
quiz.explanation: Velázquez could study the panel in the royal palace before painting “Las Meninas” in 1656.

facts.text: Jan van Eyck invented oil paint.
facts.explanation: Oil paint existed before him; he refined it with thin transparent layers.

facts.text: The dog at the couple's feet is missing from the mirror's reflection.
facts.explanation: The dog was added late and does not appear in the mirror.

facts.text: The portrait is life-size, about two meters tall.
facts.explanation: The panel is only 82 centimeters high, about the size of a pillowcase.
